title: Chapter V
paragraphs: As time passed, Mr. Earnshaw’s health began to fail. He had been active and healthy, but his strength deserted him suddenly; and once confined to his corner by the fire, he became painfully irritable. The smallest thing upset him, and any suspected challenge to his authority almost sent him into fits. This was particularly noticeable when anyone tried to cheat or bully his favourite. He guarded the boy anxiously against even an unkind word, apparently convinced that because he himself loved Heathcliff, everyone else hated him and wanted to do him harm. This did the boy no good. The kinder people among us did not want to distress the master, so we indulged his favouritism, and that indulgence fed the child’s pride and dark moods richly. Yet it became almost unavoidable. Two or three times Hindley showed his contempt in his father’s presence and drove the old man into a rage: he snatched up his stick to strike him, then trembled with fury because he lacked the strength.

At last our curate advised sending the young man to college. We had a curate then who made the income sufficient by teaching the little Lintons and Earnshaws and working his own small piece of land. Mr. Earnshaw agreed, though sorrowfully, saying, “Hindley’s good for nothing, and he’ll never prosper wherever he wanders.”

I sincerely hoped we would have peace now. It distressed me to think the master’s good deed had made him miserable. I imagined the discontent of his age and illness came from his quarrels with the family, as he insisted it did; but really, sir, it came from his failing body. Even so, we might have managed reasonably well except for two people: Miss Cathy and Joseph, the servant whom I expect you saw up there. He was, and most likely still is, the most tiresome, self-righteous Pharisee ever to rummage through a Bible, gathering its promises for himself and throwing its curses at his neighbours. His talent for sermons and pious conversation made a deep impression on Mr. Earnshaw, and the weaker the master grew, the more power Joseph gained. He never stopped pestering him about his soul and the need to govern his children strictly. He encouraged him to see Hindley as a hopeless sinner, and every night grumbled through a long list of complaints against Catherine and Heathcliff, always taking care to flatter Earnshaw’s weakness by putting the greater blame on her.

Certainly she had habits I had never seen in any other child. Fifty times a day, and more, she tried every one of us beyond patience: from the moment she came downstairs until she went to bed, we could never count on a minute without mischief. Her spirits were always at high tide and her tongue never stopped—singing, laughing and teasing everyone who would not join her. She was a wild, wicked little thing, but had the loveliest eyes, sweetest smile and lightest step in the parish. After all, I believe she meant no harm: once she made you truly cry, she nearly always cried along with you and forced you to stop so that you could comfort her. She was far too fond of Heathcliff. The worst punishment we could devise was keeping her away from him, yet she was scolded on his account more than any of us. When playing, she loved being the little mistress, giving orders and using her hands freely on her companions. She tried it on me, but I would not put up with being slapped and commanded, and I let her know it.

Now Mr. Earnshaw could not take a joke from his children: he had always been serious and strict with them. Catherine, for her part, could not understand why illness should make her father crosser and less patient than when he was strong. His peevish rebukes gave her a naughty pleasure in provoking him. Nothing delighted her more than all of us scolding her together while she defied us with a bold, impudent look and a quick reply, mocking Joseph’s religious curses and tormenting me. She also did the thing her father hated most: she showed that her pretend bullying, which he took seriously, had more power over Heathcliff than his kindness did. The boy would do anything _she_ ordered, and what _he_ ordered only when he felt inclined. Sometimes, after behaving as badly as possible all day, she came affectionately to make peace at night. “No, Cathy,” the old man would say, “I can’t love thee; thou’rt worse than thy brother. Go and say thy prayers, child, and ask God’s forgiveness. I fear thy mother and I must regret ever bringing thee up!” At first this made her cry; but constant rejection hardened her, and she laughed when I told her to apologise for her faults and ask to be forgiven.

At last the hour arrived that ended Mr. Earnshaw’s earthly troubles. One October evening he died quietly in his chair beside the fire. A strong wind battered the house and roared down the chimney. It sounded wild and stormy, but the air was not cold and we were all together. I sat a little way from the hearth with my knitting, and Joseph read his Bible near the table: in those days the servants usually sat in the main room once their work was finished. Miss Cathy had been ill, which kept her quiet. She leaned against her father’s knee, with Heathcliff lying on the floor, his head in her lap. I remember the master stroking her lovely hair before he dozed off—seeing her gentle was a rare pleasure for him—and asking, “Why canst thou not always be a good lass, Cathy?” She looked up into his face, laughed and answered, “Why can’t you always be a good man, father?” But when she saw him grow annoyed again, she kissed his hand and promised to sing him to sleep. She began very softly, until his fingers slipped from hers and his head dropped onto his chest. I told her to be quiet and keep still in case she woke him. We all remained as silent as mice for a full half-hour, and would have stayed so longer, but Joseph finished his chapter, rose, and said he must wake the master for prayers and bed. He went over, spoke his name and touched his shoulder, but he did not stir. Joseph took the candle and looked at him. I sensed something was wrong when he put the light down and, taking each child by an arm, whispered that they should “get upstairs and make little noise—they could pray on their own tonight—he’d summat to do.”

“I’ll say goodnight to father first,” Catherine said, throwing her arms round his neck before we could stop her. The poor thing understood her loss at once and screamed, “Oh, he’s dead, Heathcliff! He’s dead!” Then both children began crying with heartbreaking grief.

I wept loudly and bitterly with them, but Joseph demanded what we meant by making such a noise over a saint in heaven. He told me to put on my cloak and run to Gimmerton for the doctor and the parson. I could not see what use either could be by then. Still, I went through the wind and rain and brought one of them, the doctor, back with me; the other promised to come in the morning. Leaving Joseph to explain, I ran up to the children’s room. Their door stood ajar, and I saw they had not gone to bed, although it was after midnight. They were calmer now and did not need my comfort. The little souls were consoling each other with better thoughts than I could have found. No parson ever described heaven as beautifully as their innocent talk did; and while I listened and sobbed, I could not help wishing we were all safely there together.
